about.title: Core and fringe vocabulary
about.length_note: About 25 minutes. There are 21 short beats and 9 check questions, one idea at a time. That gives time to explain core words, fringe words, why a board needs both, and how to review a vocabulary set. I read search extracts of each source, not every page in full.

say.text: Welcome to class 3. Last time we saw the AAC toolbox. Today we look at what goes inside the tools: the words.

show.text: Core and fringe vocabulary

say.text: First, a plain word. Vocabulary means the words a person can say or choose. On an AAC board or device, it is the words that are there to pick.

show.text: Vocabulary: the words a person has available

say.text: Words come in two broad kinds. The first kind is core words: a small set of common words that make up most of what we say.

show.text: Core words: common, useful almost anywhere

say.text: Here are some examples. Go. More. Stop. Help. All done. And small pronouns like 'it'. They are short, and they fit almost any topic.

show.text: go; more; stop; help; all done; it

ask.q: Which of these is a core word?
ask.why: 'Stop' works in almost any place or topic. The other three name one specific person, thing or place.

say.text: How big is 'most'? Studies suggest a few hundred words cover about 80% of what people say. The exact figure differs a little between studies.

show.text: about 80% of what we say comes from a few hundred core words

say.text: So about four words in every five are core. The remaining fifth is where things get personal.

show.text: Roughly how much of what we say is core and fringe

ask.q: Roughly what share of what we say is made of core words?
ask.why: Studies find roughly 80% core, with fringe words making up the other 20% or so.

say.text: That other fifth is fringe words. These are specific, personal words, tied to one topic, one place or one person.

show.text: Fringe words: specific and personal

say.text: Think of names of family, friends and pets. Think of places, favourite foods and favourite shows. Some specific verbs and adjectives count too, like 'leap' or 'delicious'.

show.text: names of family, friends, pets; places; favourite foods, characters, topics; specific words like 'leap', 'delicious'

ask.q: A family's dog is called Biscuit. Is 'Biscuit' a core or a fringe word?
ask.right: Fringe: it is a specific name that matters to one person or family
wrong: Core: because it is a short word
Neither: AAC does not need names
ask.why: A name is specific and personal, which is what fringe means. AAC systems need these words too.

say.text: Why are core words so flexible? Take 'go'. Go home. Go away. Let's go! One small word, many jobs, with many people.

show.text: A speech bubble saying 'go' with four arrows leading to: home, away, a park, and a bus stop

ask.q: Why is a core word like 'go' so flexible?
ask.right: It is not tied to one topic, so it works in many places and with many people
wrong: It is the longest word on a board
Only one person can use it
ask.why: Core words are useful across all environments, so one word can serve many messages.

say.text: Fringe is the opposite. 'Biscuit' means one thing to one family. A train fan and a keen cook will each need very different fringe words.

show.text: Two boards side by side: one with train, station, ticket; one with oven, soup, basil

say.text: So a good system needs both. Core words give the frame of a message. Fringe words add the detail. 'I don't want broccoli': 'broccoli' is fringe, the rest is core.

show.text: Core (the frame): I, don't, want | Fringe (the detail): broccoli

ask.q: In 'I want more pizza', which word is the fringe word?
ask.why: 'I', 'want' and 'more' are common words that fit many messages. 'Pizza' is the specific detail.

say.text: Now picture a board with only nouns: pizza, juice, ball, cat. A person can name things and ask for them. That is about all.

show.text: A board of four large pictures: pizza, juice, ball, cat, with nothing else on it

ask.q: What would be hard to say on that board?
ask.why: Single nouns can name or ask for things. Saying stop, not, or like needs other kinds of words, mostly core.

say.text: Boards made only of requests have the same limit. Asking for things matters. But a person is more than their requests: they want to comment, refuse, joke and share news.

show.text: Nouns tend to dominate AAC vocabulary sets; adding verbs and other word types can increase acceptance and use.

say.text: The reverse also fails. With core words but no names or favourites, a person cannot talk about their own life. Most people do best with mostly core, some fringe, and a few stored phrases.

show.text: mostly core words; some fringe for important people, things and activities; a few stored social phrases

say.text: How do boards hold both? One common layout keeps core in a steady spot and swaps the fringe words to match the activity.

show.text: A board with a fixed block of core words on the left, and on the right a swappable strip: 'baking' words today, 'football' words tomorrow

ask.q: In that layout, what stays in the same place?
ask.why: Core stays constant so it is easy to learn by habit. The fringe changes with the context.

say.text: Fringe also changes over time. A person's words shift as their life, age and needs shift, so a good system lets words be added or changed.

show.text: Vocabulary changes as life changes

ask.q: A teenager using AAC starts a new job. What is a sensible step?
ask.right: Add the new people, places and work words to the fringe
wrong: Leave it: the board is finished
Remove the core words to make room
Wait a year to see if there is a problem
ask.why: A well-designed system allows vocabulary to change over time, so new people, places and interests can be added.

say.text: You do not have to add every word. Some words can be typed and spoken on the spot. Add the ones likely to come up again.

show.text: will it be used again? search for it first; type and speak it if it is a one-off; add it if it will recur

say.text: Now a skill. When you see a vocabulary set (a board, a page or an app), here are questions to ask.

show.text: 1 Are there core words like stop, more, help, go, it? 2 Is there more than nouns and requests? 3 Are this person's own people, places and favourites there? 4 Are words in the same place each time? 5 Can it change as life changes? 6 Did the person have a say?

say.text: Let's try it. A board has 40 pictures, all foods and toys.

show.text: A board of forty small pictures: pizza, cake, juice, teddy, ball, car and similar items, with no small words

ask.q: What is the best first question to ask about this board?
ask.right: Where are words like stop, more and help that work everywhere?
wrong: How many pictures could fit on one page?
ask.why: All nouns and requests is the common gap. Core words are what let a person say far more.

say.text: One caution. Every person is different. A speech-language pathologist can look at one person's needs and help choose and order words. This class is general learning, not clinical advice.

show.text: Ask a speech-language pathologist about one person's words

say.text: To sum up: core words are few, common and flexible. Fringe words are many, specific and personal. A good system has both and grows with the person. Next class: symbol sets and page layouts.

show.text: core: common, flexible; fringe: specific, personal; both needed; vocabulary changes over time; ask the six questions

notes.topic: Questions to ask about a vocabulary set

other_side.claim: Core words should be the heart of an AAC vocabulary.
other_side.other_view: Most experts agree. Some warn against forcing core words when there are urgent needs that fringe words could meet right away. Motivating, personal words can build engagement, and core words can then be modelled around them. Others say the core/fringe split can miss useful words, such as relational words, so lists alone are not enough.

other_side.claim: About 80% of what we say is core, so a few hundred words are enough.
other_side.other_view: The 80% figure is a rough guide. Studies and word lists differ in size and in who was sampled. Some authors note that core words are not always the most motivating to use. Fringe words, though used less often, are what make a message about the person's own life. One reader comment on a PrAACtical AAC post says that core vocabulary was the last to be lost in semantic dementia, so those patients needed fringe words instead. That is a single anecdote, not research.
